#8685. LLM Misuse Safeguards Rely on Untrusted Input: A Widespread, High-Risk Vulnerability

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (223 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

LLM Misuse Safeguards Rely on Untrusted Input: A Widespread, High-Risk Vulnerability

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (223 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2607.27951v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models now help professionals in fields such as cybersecurity and biology, yet the same answers would help an attacker. Deployers rely on misuse safeguards to keep such answers from attackers. We find that these safeguards share a high-risk vulnerability: they decide whether to release an answer from what users write, including the professional identity or purpose they claim, and anyone can write such a claim. Threat reports from model vendors and security firms show that attackers who fabricate a professional identity or purpose already exploit this vulnerability to cause serious harm. The vulnerability is also widespread across the state of the art: every defense proposed in 129 papers from the latest editions of 12 top venues has it. Safeguard research studies the wrong object: it treats harm as a property of the text of a request, although the same text can come from a professional or an attacker. Current safeguard benchmarks therefore cannot reveal the vulnerability: a safeguard can score high on them and still give dangerous answers to attackers. Because the vulnerability lies in what users write, no improvement in how safeguards judge that writing can close it. Under the patch we propose, large language models can help professionals without giving dangerous capabilities to anyone who merely claims to be one.

Latest Update: How ISVs are unlocking European workloads using Google Cloud Dedicated technology

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across Europe, organizations handling sensitive workloads in regulated sectors — such as financial services, healthcare, critical infrastructure, and the public sector — are trying to modernize their infrastructure while adhering to strict local data governance standards, including SecNumCloud in France and BSI C3A in Germany.
  • In a recent development, to help organizations accomplish this, Google Cloud Dedicated provides the architectural, security, and API consistency of Google Cloud in locally governed environments managed by independent domestic operators.
  • To meet regional sovereignty requirements, organizations acquire and run these software solutions through trusted local entities — such as S3NS in France (a joint venture majority-owned and managed by Thales) and a newly formed German entity that will also be owned and managed by Thales, currently in preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Product Lead, Google Cloud Dedicated.

Product Manager, Google Cloud Dedicated.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Across Europe, organizations handling sensitive workloads in regulated sectors — such as financial services, healthcare, critical infrastructure, and the public sector — are trying to modernize their infrastructure while adhering to strict local data governance standards, including SecNumCloud in France and BSI C3A in Germany.

In a recent development, to help organizations accomplish this, Google Cloud Dedicated provides the architectural, security, and API consistency of Google Cloud in locally governed environments managed by independent domestic operators. But infrastructure is only the starting point. Organizations also need to transform the software ecosystem they rely on every day.

To meet regional sovereignty requirements, organizations acquire and run these software solutions through trusted local entities — such as S3NS in France (a joint venture majority-owned and managed by Thales) and a newly formed German entity that will also be owned and managed by Thales, currently in preview. These local entities operate dedicated infrastructure stacks, help maintain operational custody, and handle customer data within independent jurisdictional boundaries.

Today, we are highlighting the expanding independent software vendor (ISV) ecosystem validated on Google Cloud Dedicated, enabling French and German organizations to run their critical enterprise software in environments designed to support their sovereign and regulatory needs.

Deploying in a sovereign boundary should not require an organization to sacrifice software choice or rewrite its enterprise applications.Because Google Cloud Dedicated provides architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, validated enterprise software runs directly inside these partner-operated environments without custom re-platforming.

This model provides European enterprises with three concrete advantages:.

Localized operational custody: Infrastructure operations, software quarantine procedures, and day-to-day administrative access are under the direct management of local European partners operating with specialized remote technical escalations governed by strict, partner-supervised escorted access controls.

Broad software choice: Regulated institutions can deploy industry-standard tools for identity governance, cyber resilience, simulation, and data streaming natively in their sovereign perimeter.

Streamlined compliance: Organizations fulfill national frameworks like SecNumCloud and BSI guidelines while preserving familiar CI/CD pipelines, APIs, and developer workflows.

When highly regulated European institutions consider moving to a sovereign cloud, the infrastructure itself is rarely the primary roadblock. The real bottleneck is software.Historically, pursuing strict sovereignty meant accepting compromises:.

Rewriting applications from scratch or maintaining custom, brittle tooling because mainstream enterprise platforms were unavailable.

Forcing security, engineering, and data teams to abandon the industry-standard tools they use daily in favor of untested niche alternatives.

Sidelining high-impact initiatives like real-time fraud scoring, automated DevSecOps, and modern identity governance simply because the required ISVs could not legally or technically operate in the environment.

Because Google Cloud Dedicated maintains architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, leading global and European software providers can deploy their proven platforms directly inside national, domestic operator-managed boundaries. Regulated organizations retain the software, automated pipelines, and operational standards they rely on — without sacrificing compliance or operational custody.

Deploying enterprise software on Google Cloud Dedicated and S3NS isn't just about hosting an application locally; it’s about pairing proven software engines with sovereign operations. Here is how these joint architectures unlock strategic value for European enterprises:.

Cohesity on Google Cloud Dedicated (Sovereign cyber resilience): Cohesity has many options to meet organizational data sovereignty objectives, whether on-premises or in the cloud with Google Cloud Dedicated. This is done through a unified, cyber resilient, AI-powered data platform — Cohesity Data Cloud — that is sovereign-by-design, making it easier to protect, manage, recover, and have visibility into data, while supporting compliance with data sovereignty requirements. For example, running Cohesity directly in the S3NS perimeter combines Cohesity’s Zero Trust cyber resilience architecture designed for immutability with local operational custody. Customers gain advanced threat hunting, cyber vaulting, and recovery orchestration that powers quick, clean, and trusted cyber-recovery from ransomware threats without allowing diagnostic telemetry, secondary backup copies, or operational keys to traverse external networks.

In a recent development, gitLab on Google Cloud Dedicated (Secure, compliant software delivery pipelines): Combining GitLab’s DevSecOps platform with Google Cloud Dedicated allows defense, aerospace, and public sector engineering teams to ship code at commercial velocity. Proprietary source code, vulnerability scans, and CI/CD artifact registries stay contained behind the partner-operated boundary, significantly reducing audit friction of using public SaaS code repositories.

It has been revealed that ansys, part of Synopsys, on Google Cloud Dedicated (High-performance sovereign engineering simulation): Pairing Ansys, part of Synopsys, high-performance computing simulation workflows with the dedicated compute clusters of Google Cloud Dedicated gives European manufacturers the massive scale needed for aerodynamic, fluid, and structural modeling. Highly sensitive intellectual property, blueprints, and digital twins designed to keep intellectual property within regional boundaries and national jurisdiction while running at cloud speed.

According to recent reports, memority on Google Cloud Dedicated / S3NS (Audit-ready sovereign identity governance): Integrating Memority’s identity factory platform directly into the S3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment provides regulated entities with capabilities designed to support their NIS2 and DORA compliance requirements with the PREMI3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment. Organizations can manage and audit millions of identities without building custom IAM infrastructure or exposing access tokens to non-European cloud services."Our customers — from critical infrastructure operators to financial institutions — share the same requirement: an enterprise-grade IAM platform capable of managing millions of identities while meeting the highest standards of digital sovereignty. As NIS2 and DORA reshape the regulatory landscape, this requirement has become a business-critical imperative. S3NS enables us to address it at scale by providing a comprehensive IAM platform hosted in a SecNumCloud-qualified cloud environment, with built-in capabilities supporting the auditability, traceability, and operational resilience expected under these regulations,” stated Francis Grégoire, Deputy CEO, Memority.

RackWare on Google Cloud Dedicated (De-risked cloud migration): Running RackWare’s automated migration and disaster recovery engines on Google Cloud Dedicated gives organizations a low-friction bridge from on-premises data centers into sovereign cloud environments. Teams can replicate, synchronize, and failover complex enterprise operating environments, bypassing the prohibitive cost and timeline of manual application refactoring.

Striim on Google Cloud Dedicated (Real-time data streaming without jurisdictional risk): Combining Striim’s continuous change data capture engine with the local boundaries of Google Cloud Dedicated enables organizations to feed live operational analytics and fraud models without batch delays. Financial institutions and logistics leaders can stream sensitive customer and payment transactions in sub-second intervals, with strong technical assurances that streaming pipelines remain bound to local infrastructure."Regulated organizations should not have to choose between modern, real-time data and the control their environments demand. By making Striim available on Google Cloud Dedicated, we can help customers securely move and continuously deliver trusted data to the systems that power critical operations, analytics, and AI without ever compromising on sovereignty or resilience,” said Phillip Cockrell, SVP of Business Development, Striim.UPS Capital integrated Striim’s real-time streaming technology with analytics models to power its DeliveryDefense address verification and delivery security system. By streaming and validating transaction and delivery data continuously without batch lag, UPS assesses risk scoring in real time — a capability European logistics and financial operators can now deploy directly in their sovereign boundary.

Industry observers note that red Hat on Google Cloud Dedicated (Operational consistency on open hybrid platforms): Deploying Red Hat Enterprise Linux and OpenShift across Google Cloud Dedicated bridges on-premises infrastructure and sovereign cloud environments. Engineering teams maintain their existing operating runtimes, container standards, and administrative toolsets across sites, avoiding vendor lock-in and eliminating the operational retraining typically required when moving to sovereign stacks.

It has been revealed that saviynt on Google Cloud Dedicated (Zero-trust access governance across sovereign assets): Deploying Saviynt’s privileged access management and identity governance inside the sovereign boundary allows enterprises to centrally enforce least-privilege security across critical databases and workloads. Security administrators maintain automated role lifecycles and complete audit logs without exposing access intelligence to offshore management planes.

Tsuga on Google Cloud Dedicated (Telemetry and observability): Tsuga’s bring-your-own-cloud (BYOC) observability platform deployed inside a customer's dedicated VPC resolves one of the biggest security exposures in regulated IT: transmitting production telemetry to third-party SaaS monitoring providers. By processing all traces, metrics, and logs on local storage, organizations achieve full observability, reduce external data egress costs, and help protect sensitive operational data.

MongoDB on Google Cloud Dedicated (Modern data velocity with domestic residency): Running MongoDB Enterprise Advanced on Google Cloud Dedicated gives developers the flexibility of the document model while adhering to strict regional isolation requirements. Regulated organizations can rapidly build modern, real-time applications and customer portals using modern development patterns without being forced onto legacy relational database architectures.

According to recent reports, ispirer on Google Cloud Dedicated (Automated legacy modernization): Pairing Ispirer’s automated database conversion toolkit with Google Cloud Dedicated addresses a key friction point in database modernization: the complexity of migrating legacy database engines. Automated code and schema conversion shrinks complex multi-year migration timelines into predictable, low-risk deployments on modern sovereign infrastructure."Every migration is really a risk decision. Offering the Ispirer toolkit on Google Cloud Dedicated gives customers over 27 years of deterministic conversion experience—that's the value we consistently hear back from client teams,” mentioned Natallia Bespalova, CEO, Ispirer Systems.

Splunk integration with Google Cloud Dedicated (sovereign log collection, observability, and SIEM integration): Splunk now supports Google Cloud Dedicated as a first-class log source. Extensions to the open-source OpenTelemetry Collector allow organizations to export logs from Google Cloud Dedicated environments into Splunk Enterprise using the Google Cloud Pub/Sub receiver and the Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC) exporter, alongside enhancements to the Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud for direct log collection Additionally, Splunk Observability Cloud now supports Google Cloud Dedicated through its Infrastructure Monitoring cloud integration, which connects projects to pull metrics and metadata from services so teams can monitor resource and application health. Critical infrastructure and financial institutions can now centralize security analytics, performance monitoring, SIEM operations, and incident response while keeping audit logs, threat intelligence, and sensitive operational telemetry within national boundaries.

Sources indicate that solo.io on Google Cloud Dedicated (Kubernetes-native governance and runtime for AI agents): kagent from Solo.io adds a Kubernetes-native runtime for AI agents and their MCP tool servers on Google Cloud Dedicated, declared and governed through the same GitOps and RBAC workflows platform teams already operate. Lifecycle control, agent-level access policy, and human-in-the-loop approval are built in, helping organizations ensure agents are deployed, audited, and managed within the local partner perimeter.

In a recent development, pelico on Google Cloud Dedicated (Sovereign supply chain resilience for aerospace and defense): Running Pelico on Google Cloud Dedicated with S3NS PREMI3NS gives industrial manufacturers the ability to turn ERP and planning data into clear operational priorities while keeping sensitive data under European sovereign control. Proven for a global aerospace and defense group, this architecture lets sovereignty-minded organizations anticipate and resolve supply chain disruptions using the capabilities of Pelico’s cloud offering, without compromising strict regional isolation or domestic operational custody.

Latest Update: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2607.23624v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

#8679. OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (209 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (209 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2607.16235v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are proprietary, and leading wearable foundation models trained on them are rarely open weight or include reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we introduce OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive wearable health dataset broadly accessible to qualified researchers, alongside open-source implementations and weights for recent wearable foundation models. Derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, OpenMHC comprises over 67M participant-hours of wearable recordings across up to 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 170 health, lifestyle, mood, and behavioral variables from 11,894 participants. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark for standardized evaluation across three tasks: (1) health and behavioral outcome prediction, (2) multivariate data imputation, and (3) time-series forecasting. Benchmarking classical methods alongside recent wearable and time-series foundation models, we find that while foundation models perform strongly, carefully tuned classical baselines like XGBoost remain highly competitive. By uniting broad-access wearable data with open code and model weights, OpenMHC provides a framework needed to drive reproducible advances in wearable health AI.

#8676. Adapting Generalist Vehicle Models for High-Speed MPC Across Terrains

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Adapting Generalist Vehicle Models for High-Speed MPC Across Terrains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2607.13319v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-speed off-road autonomy requires precise closed-loop control for a target vehicle while remaining robust across changing terrains. Recent forward kinodynamic (FKD) prediction foundation models suggest a promising path, starting from a generalist model and specializing it to the target platform. However, effective specialization remains challenging, as it often requires substantial real-world data, and models adapted to one setting can still overfit to specific terrains or driving regimes. We present OptCar (Optimized Car), a recipe for bridging the gap from generalist to specialist FKD models that preserves cross-terrain generalization while optimizing performance for a specific vehicle. OptCar introduces a transformer FKD architecture that uses FiLM to condition multi-step predictions on a single dynamics context token summarizing recent state-action history. It then specializes the generalist model using limited real-world data and targeted synthetic rollouts from environment-specific system identification. In closed-loop model predictive control (MPC) experiments across three terrains and an out-of-distribution cart-pulling task, the largest gains appear at 6 m/s, the highest speed evaluated and the regime in which slip dominates tracking error. On vegetation + dirt, the most slip-diverse terrain, OptCar reduces 6 m/s trajectory tracking error by roughly 55% relative to AnyCar fine-tuned on real data alone, and remains the most accurate even when an unseen cart payload changes the dynamics. With 5 minutes of real data per terrain, OptCar is competitive on road with a specialist trained on 30 minutes of road data and outperforms it when the terrain changes. Project Page : https://amrl.cs.utexas.edu/optcar/.

Real-time fall detection based on vision for low-power edge platforms

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2607.12909v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Falling detection is vital for elderly care and intelligent surveillance; however, prevailing vision-based approaches predominantly frame it as static pose classification or discrete temporal pattern matching, fundamentally overlooking the instability dynamics of the human support system. This paper proposes a physics-informed falling detection framework that recasts falling as a stability-loss event in a coupled dynamical system. We introduce a novel dual-LTC architecture comprising a Center-of-Mass (CoM) subsystem and a Base-of-Support (BoS) subsystem, both instantiated as Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) neural networks to continuously model inertial trajectory evolution and ground-contact adjustment through adaptive time constants, Physical interpretability of falling motion. A learnable coupling module emulates physical interaction between the two subsystems, while a Stability Manifold classifier operates in the joint latent space to detect boundary crossing via Lyapunov-inspired stability metrics. Complementary counterfactual trajectory projection and Time-to-Collision (TTC) estimation further enable irreversibility assessment and early warning. The architecture is designed to support a three-state prediction paradigm (Normal, Falling, Fallen); in this preliminary study, we validate the core stability discrimination capability on a two-class dataset (Normal vs. Falling), leaving the full three-state temporal transition to future work. Unlike conventional CNN--RNN pipelines, the proposed formulation encodes continuous-time mechanical inertia, yielding a sub-50K-parameter network capable of real-time inference on resource-constrained edge devices. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive accuracy with superior physical interpretability, validating its efficacy for low-compute visual fall detection.

Statistical Adversaries: Natural Backdoor-like Adversarial Features in Clean Vision Datasets

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (165 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2607.05516v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Model-specific adversarial attacks have been extensively studied. We study a different failure mode: naturally occurring statistical signals in vision data that can behave as backdoor-like triggers without being maliciously inserted. We call these signals statistical adversaries. We analyse ImageNet to find patterns that are strongly linked to certain labels. We then use statistical controls to remove random correlations from our candidate signals. Finally, we demonstrate that these signals directly and predictably alter model predictions. These statistical adversaries are more targeted than generic corruptions and transfer across different model architectures. This suggests that some vulnerabilities are driven by dataset structure and distribution rather than a single model's idiosyncrasies. We conclude that ordinary datasets can contain exploitable adversarial surfaces even in the absence of poisoning, and suggest that dataset audits should treat spurious structure not only as a source of bias or interpretability failure, but also as a latent attack surface for vision models.

Localized LoRA-MoE: Mixture of Low-Rank Experts With Adaptive Routing

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2607.05114v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA adapt large models through a single low-rank revision. Such updates are susceptible to gradient interference: when a training stream interleaves multiple operational contexts, conflicting updates to shared adapter weights collapse the adapter into an unspecialized average. While recent methods introduce block-wise isolation to remedy this glitch, their topologies are static and cannot adapt to context switching or localized sensor degradation. In this work, we introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that combines localized spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing. We propose and evaluate two architectural variants: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE (centralized routing), which modulates the entire structural grid through a single context-conditioned gate, and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE (decentralized routing), which assigns an independent gate to every coordinate cell of the matrix grid. Across three structured transformation benchmarks--a high-dimensional SVD matrix simulation, context-switched transformations over real tabular data, and spatial reconstruction under simulated sensor occlusion--both variants outperform static baselines under comparable adapter budgets. Both variants perform similarly when context shifts the grid uniformly, while cell-wise routing is strictly better when contexts are spatially heterogeneous. When fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing at a fixed adapter budget outperforms LoRA and static localized adapters, matching per-task adapters with 6x budgets. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both routed variants outperform static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving +3.9 points over LoRA at matched active capacity.

Spatiotemporal and Multi-Robot Motion Planning on Graphs of Space-Time Convex Sets

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (220 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2607.00444v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decoupled multi-robot motion planning avoids the high-dimensional joint configuration space but requires repeated single-robot planning among moving obstacles, where route choice and timing are coupled. We develop a framework based on graphs of space-time convex sets (ST-GCSs) for continuous spatiotemporal planning and multi-robot coordination. An ST-GCS represents collision-free space-time by convex sets, allowing the sequence of regions and the geometry and timing of piecewise-linear trajectories to be optimized jointly under velocity limits. To incorporate moving obstacles and previously planned robots, we develop Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD), which removes their swept occupancies while maintaining a convex decomposition for subsequent planning queries. Building on path-based GCS search, we develop a best-first solver tailored to the ST-GCS motion model, exploiting temporal reachability for dominance pruning and using admissible heuristics with separate or joint search-key evaluation. Precomputed heuristic bounds can also be reused across reservation-updated graphs. We integrate ST-GCS planning and ECD into prioritized multi-robot planning and introduce windowed coordination with dynamic window adjustment to limit reservation-induced graph growth. Experiments demonstrate improved scalability and competitive solution quality against optimization-based and sampling-based planners on challenging spatiotemporal and multi-robot problems. Large-scale simulations coordinate up to $100$ robots within a minute, while real-robot demonstrations showcase the practical applicability of the framework. Project homepage: https://sites.google.com/view/stgcs.

The Language-Energy Divide: Measuring Energy Costs of Multilingual LLM Inference

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2606.21869v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multilingual settings, yet the energy costs of serving these models across different languages remain poorly understood. We present a systematic study of inference energy consumption across languages with ML.Energy framework (Chung et al., 2026). We find striking disparities: energy consumption per output token varies by up to 8.3 times across languages, while total energy for a fixed set of requests varies by up to 179 times between the cheapest (English, 17.6 kJ) and the most expensive (Pashto, 3,147 kJ) languages. Our analysis highlights that this disparity is driven by two compounding factors: (1) higher per-token energy costs for languages using complex or rare scripts, and (2) more tokens generated for low-resource languages. Moreover, we find a double cost + performance penalty: languages with the highest energy footprints also tend to achieve the lowest task accuracy. We reveal that the energy divide persists across models, hardware, and tasks, suggesting a systemic energy inequity in multilingual LLM deployment. Finally, we recommend that the community treat energy as a first-class evaluation axis, extend reporting checklists and model cards to include it, and adopt deployment-side mitigations for better energy efficiency.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2606.17541v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Offline evaluation of agentic systems often collapses trajectories into a binary terminal success value, discarding information about partial progress. This, in turn, results in widespread ties that create statistical inefficiency by reducing effective sample size and weakening the ability to distinguish systems. We propose preference-based trajectory evaluation, an evaluation measure that compares pairs of trajectories directly by using temporal preferences between time-to-return profiles. We find that, across diverse agentic and interactive benchmarks, success-based metrics result in tied comparisons on roughly 75% of instances, while trajectory-aware preferences reduce ties to roughly 35%, improving discriminative power, ranking stability, and data efficiency. Our results suggest that benchmark saturation, often portrayed as the result of poor data collection or problem difficulty, may also be explained by the design of the evaluation measure.

Tech Report: FoundCause: A Foundation Model for Causal Discovery with Latent Confounders from Observational Data

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (191 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2606.17516v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data requires recovering directed relations and latent confounding without interventions. We propose FoundCause, an {\em amortized causal discovery foundation model} trained only on synthetic structural causal models that maps datasets to causal graphs in a single forward pass. A permutation-equivariant transformer alternates attention over samples and variables to model cross-variable dependence and per-variable distributions. Pairwise dependence and asymmetry statistics guide its attention, edge decoder and confounder module. The decoder separates edge existence from direction, while triangular refinement incorporates evidence from chains and colliders. Learnable latent tokens predict which variable pairs share a hidden common cause, and a masked input representation handles missing data. To our knowledge, FoundCause is the first amortized causal discovery approach for i.i.d. observational data to predict latent confounding as a separate, explicit output. On 14 real-world and semi-synthetic datasets, FoundCause leads 11 classical and 7 amortized baselines in average AUROC, $F_1$, skeleton $F_1$, and normalized structural Hamming distance ($\mathrm{SHD}/d$): clearly in $\mathrm{SHD}/d$ ($0.875$ vs.\ $0.956$), narrowly in $F_1$ ($0.531$ vs.\ $0.516$). It also has the highest accuracy among amortized methods on bivariate cause--effect pairs.

These directions are usually discovered through indirect learning objectives such as sparse reconstruction, but it remains unclear what existing statistical structure distinguishes interpretable directions and whether that structure can be used directly for feature discovery. Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, we find that (1) the recovered non-Gaussian directions capture coherent lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns under both human and LLM-based evaluation; (2) non-Gaussianity is positively associated with both human-label confidence and automated interpretability; and (3) the resulting coordinates are competitive with SAEs across interpretability, sparse reconstruction, concept prediction, and causal interventions, while fitting in minutes per layer and using 7-43 times less memory. These results show that non-Gaussianity is a direct unsupervised signal for discovering interpretable and useful structure in activations.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2606.04493v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When shown matches between two photographs of the same cathedral, people can tell at a glance which ones are wrong: a window matched to its look-alike jumps against its neighbors, while correct matches shift together. Two-view correspondence learning, also called correspondence pruning, asks a network to make this judgment for thousands of candidate matches, most of which are wrong. Mamba, a fast sequence model, now drives strong pruners, but it reads the matches as a plain sequence, and whether its scan can capture such agreement is unclear. We propose SFMambaNet, which scans the matches cluster by cluster, so that correct matches vary slowly along the sequence while wrong ones stay erratic, and filters the scanned features with learnable frequency-domain gates between its forward and backward passes. On camera pose estimation, outlier removal and homography estimation, we find that SFMambaNet outperforms spatial-domain Mamba baselines with about two million parameters. Contrary to the usual expectation that such gains come from extra capacity, we find that a parameter-free low-pass filter beats point-wise layers as large as the gates. The learned gates turn low-pass on their own and make the scan far less sensitive to how the matches are shuffled. Together, these results show that frequency is a natural language for describing agreement between correspondences, with implications for other sequence models that must read unordered sets, such as point clouds and graphs.

In a recent development, arXiv:2605.25267v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) adapts online from interaction history without test-time parameter updates while controlling episode cost under a safety budget. Under out-of-distribution (OOD) deployment shifts, pretraining-only safe ICRL can give poor reward-safety tradeoffs because the remaining budget affects behavior only through frozen policy conditioning, not an explicit action-level check against predicted future cost. We propose a latent Q-Barrier shield that learns a context representation, latent dynamics, and an ensemble cost critic before deployment. Without parameter updates, the shield infers context from history and filters or softly reweights candidate actions using the remaining budget and predicted future cost. We prove a conditional one-step barrier-margin bound over realized candidate sets, with explicit Bellman and latent-prediction error terms. Across five safe ICRL benchmarks, the shield improves deployment-time reward-safety tradeoffs over a strong safe-ICRL baseline: after a short context window, it achieves higher return in four of five benchmarks while matching or lowering average episode cost in all five. arXiv:2605.21752v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recommender systems trained on user interaction data are susceptible to behavioral intensity imbalance--a systematic distortion arising from heterogeneous engagement patterns across consumers. This imbalance skews feedback signals such that observed interactions no longer faithfully reflect true preferences, causing models to disproportionately amplify signals from highly active users while underrepresenting others, which ultimately degrades recommendation quality and robustness at scale. To address this problem, we propose a nonparametric contrastive percentile approximation framework, PEARL, that models relative preference signals instead of absolute engagement magnitudes. Building upon relative advantage debiasing, PEARL leverages real contrastive interaction samples to approximate percentile relationships directly, without relying on auxiliary distribution estimation models. We provide theoretical justification demonstrating that such pairwise comparisons yield unbiased estimates of percentile-based preference signals. For broader applicability, we introduce a prediction-based bootstrapping mechanism for percentile smoothing to handle sparse and discrete feedback, alongside a generalized value-weighted formulation and a co-training strategy to enhance both modeling flexibility and representation learning. Extensive offline experiments demonstrate that PEARL effectively mitigates behavioral bias and consistently improves recommendation performance across multiple ranking targets. Deployed in a production livestream platform with a combined user base of billions, online A/B testing confirms substantial real-world gains: +2.10% Watch Duration, +0.80% Consumption Amount, +1.49% Interaction Rate, and -6.91% Report Rate.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2605.20730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models (LLMs) to adapt to fresh tasks through demonstrations, yet it suffers from escalating inference costs as context length increases. While task vectors offer a promising alternative by compressing demonstrations into compact hidden-state representations, their quality has been evaluated only through downstream task accuracy. This indirect criterion provides limited insight into how to design more effective task vector extraction methods. In this paper, we posit that inference using task vectors should align their predictive distribution with that of ICL. To quantify this, we introduce $d_{\text{NTP}}$, a metric that measures the discrepancy in next-token probabilities between task vector-based and ICL-based inference. Our empirical analysis reveals that $d_{\text{NTP}}$ serves as a performance proxy, exhibiting a strong negative correlation with downstream accuracy. Motivated by this, we develop Linear Task Vector (LTV), a method designed to minimize $d_{\text{NTP}}$ via a closed-form linear mapping that estimates demonstration effects through regression. Across eight classification benchmarks and five LLMs, LTV consistently outperforms existing task vector baselines, improving average accuracy by 9.2\% while reducing inference latency. We further show that LTV outperforms the baselines on regression tasks. Moreover, we investigate the transferability of LTV across different model scales; an aspect that has remained nascent in task vector research. Specifically, we empirically show that task vectors from a larger model can enhance a smaller model's performance by 6.4\%, suggesting a new utility for extracted task representations.

However, its practical adoption in industrial e-commerce search remains challenging, given the massive and dynamic product catalogs, strict latency requirements, and the need to align retrieval with downstream ranking goals. In this work, we propose a retrieval framework tailored for real-world recall scenarios, positioning generative retrieval as a recall-stage supplement rather than an end-to-end replacement. Our method, CQ-SID (Category-and-Query constrained Semantic ID), employs category-aware and query-item contrastive learning along with Residual Quantized VAEs to encode items into hierarchical semantic cluster identifiers, significantly reducing beam search complexity. Additionally, we develop EG-GRPO (Expert-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization), a reinforcement learning approach that aligns generative recall with downstream ranking under sparse rewards by injecting ground-truth samples to stabilize training. Offline experiments on TmallAPP search logs show that CQ-SID achieves up to 26.76% and 11.11% relative gains in semantic and personalized click hitrate over RQ-VAE baselines, while halving beam search size. EG-GRPO further improves multi-objective performance. Online A/B tests confirm gains in GMV (+1.15%) and UCTCVR (+0.40%). The generative recall channel now contributes substantially in production, accounting for over 50.25% of exposures, 58.96% of clicks, and 72.63% of purchases, demonstrating a viable path for deploying generative retrieval in real-world e-commerce systems.

Tech Report: AgentLens: Revealing The Lucky Pass Problem in SWE-Agent Evaluation

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (255 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Industry observers note that arXiv:2605.12925v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluation of software engineering (SWE) agents is dominated by a binary signal: whether the final patch passes the tests. This outcome-only view treats a principled solution and a chaotic trial-and-error process as equivalent. We show that this equivalence is empirically false. We evaluate 2,614 OpenHands trajectories from eight model backends on 60 SWE-bench Verified tasks. Of these, 47 have enough passing trajectories to construct task-level process references, yielding a 1,815-trajectory evaluation subset. Among passing trajectories in this subset, 10.7% exhibit behavior we call a Lucky Pass: regression cycles, blind retries, missing verification, or temporally disordered exploration, implementation, and verification. We introduce AgentLens, a framework for process-level assessment of SWE-agent trajectories, and release AgentLens-Bench, a dataset of 1,815 trajectories annotated with quality scores, waste signals, divergence points, and 47 task-level Prefix Tree Acceptor (PTA) references. AgentLens builds PTA references by merging multiple passing solutions for the same task, and uses a context-sensitive intent labeler to assign actions to Exploration, Implementation, Verification, or Orchestration based on trajectory history rather than tool identity alone. On AgentLens-Bench, the quality score separates passing trajectories into Lucky, Solid, and Ideal tiers and further decomposes Lucky Passes into five recurring mechanisms. Across the eight model backends, Lucky rates range from 0.5% to 23.2%, and some models move by as many as five rank positions when ranked by quality score instead of pass rate. We publicly release AgentLens-Bench and the AgentLens SDK at https://github.com/agentlens-framework/agentlens, with a project page at https://agentlens-framework.github.io/agentlens/.

arXiv:2605.11654v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The low-altitude economy is growing rapidly, increasing demand for reliable drone navigation. Common tasks such as delivery, inspection, and search-and-rescue rely on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), which can be jammed, spoofed, or unavailable. Cross-view geo-localization (CVGL), which matches an oblique drone view to a geo-referenced satellite tile, offers an alternative for autonomous localization when GNSS fails. However, current CVGL methods have three limitations: (1) global descriptors compress patch grids into a single vector, without separating cross-view-shared layout from view-specific texture; (2) altitude-related scale variation remains in the learned embedding instead of being marginalized as a nuisance; and (3) multi-objective training uses hand-tuned loss weights despite incompatible gradient scales. We propose SKYPART, a lightweight, swappable head for patch-based vision transformers (ViTs) that explicitly groups patches into parts. It combines (i) learnable prototypes that compete for patch tokens through single-pass cosine assignment; (ii) altitude-conditioned linear modulation used only during training, yielding altitude-free retrieval embeddings at inference; (iii) graph-attention readout over active prototypes; and (iv) Kendall uncertainty-weighted multi-objective learning that learns loss-group weights end-to-end. With 26.95M parameters and 22.14 GFLOPs, SKYPART is the smallest top-performing method in our comparison and achieves state-of-the-art results on SUES-200, University-1652, and DenseUAV using single-pass retrieval without reranking or test-time augmentation (TTA). Its accuracy advantage over the strongest baseline further increases under ten WeatherPrompt corruption conditions. Code: https://github.com/chisngyen/SkyPart.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (235 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2605.09238v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Muon and related norm-constrained optimizers, now central to large-scale learning, compute updates via a linear maximization oracle (LMO) over a matrix-norm ball in Euclidean space. However, they do not generalize cleanly to manifold-valued parameters such as low-rank factorizations, orthogonality constraints, or symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrices. Naively restricting the Muon LMO to the tangent space (i) breaks quotient symmetries and (ii) couples the tangent-space constraint with an ambient norm bound, which obstructs closed-form solutions. We resolve both complications with a key observation: every Riemannian metric canonically lifts a unitarily invariant Euclidean norm to an intrinsic norm on each tangent space. The resulting intrinsic LMO is symmetry preserving and, under a structural condition on the scaled tangent space, reduces to a standard Euclidean LMO. Building on this, we introduce intrinsic Muon (iMuon), a unified framework with closed-form updates on the fixed-rank, SPD, Stiefel, and Grassmann manifolds for various unitarily invariant norms, including the spectral, Frobenius, and nuclear norms. We establish deterministic and stochastic convergence rates of iMuon with constants that depend only on the manifold dimension. Notably, on the fixed-rank manifold, the constant depends only on the rank, which makes the rate independent of factor conditioning and removes the runtime factor rescaling required by prior work. Experiments on LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs, image classification, and subspace learning illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2605.07830v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in offensive cybersecurity. In this paper, we reveal an interesting phenomenon: different agents exhibit distinct attack patterns. Specifically, agents exhibit distinct attack-selection biases, differing in both the families they explore and the concentration of their efforts. These patterns remain relatively stable across prompt variations. To systematically quantify this behavior, we introduce CyBiasBench, a comprehensive 630-session benchmark that evaluates five agents on three targets and four prompt conditions with ten attack families. We identify explicit bias across agents, with different dominant attack families and varying entropy levels in their attack-family allocation distributions. Such bias characterizes agent behavior within the evaluated environments and provides information beyond aggregate attack success rates. Furthermore, our experiments reveal a bias momentum effect, where agents resist explicit steering toward attack families that conflict with their bias. This forced distribution shift does not yield measurable improvements in attack performance. To ensure reproducibility and facilitate future research, we release an interactive result dashboard at https://trustworthyai.co.kr/CyBiasBench/ and a reproducibility artifact with aggregated session-level statistics and full evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Harry24k/CyBiasBench.

arXiv:2604.22774v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate transcription of handwritten mathematics is crucial for educational AI systems, yet current benchmarks fail to evaluate this capability properly. Most prior studies focus on single-line expressions and rely on lexical metrics such as BLEU, which fail to assess the semantic reasoning across multi-line student solutions. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of multi-line handwritten math Optical Character Recognition (OCR), revealing a critical failure mode of Vision-Language Models (VLMs): over-correction. Instead of faithfully transcribing a student's work, these models often "fix" errors, thereby hiding the very mistakes an educational assessment aims to detect. To address this, we propose PINK (Penalized INK-based score), a semantic evaluation metric that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) for rubric-based grading and explicitly penalizes over-correction. Our comprehensive evaluation of 15 state-of-the-art VLMs on the FERMAT dataset reveals substantial ranking reversals compared to BLEU: models like GPT-4o are heavily penalized for aggressive over-correction, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash emerges as the most faithful transcriber. Furthermore, human expert studies show that PINK aligns significantly better with human judgment (55.0% preference over BLEU's 39.5%), providing a more reliable evaluation framework for handwritten math OCR in educational settings. Code is available at https://github.com/9115jin/PINK.

We present the Women's Health Benchmark (WHBench), a targeted evaluation suite of 47 expert-crafted scenarios across 10 women's health topics, designed to expose clinically meaningful failure modes including outdated guidelines, unsafe omissions, dosing errors, and equity-related blind spots. We evaluate 22 models using a 23-criterion rubric spanning clinical accuracy, completeness, safety, communication quality, instruction following, equity, uncertainty handling, and guideline adherence, with safety-weighted penalties and server-side score recalculation. Across 3,102 attempted responses (3,100 scored), no model mean performance exceeds 75 percent; the best model reaches 72.1 percent. Even top models show low fully correct rates and substantial variation in harm rates. Inter-rater reliability is moderate at the response label level but high for model ranking, supporting WHBench utility for comparative system evaluation while highlighting the need for expert oversight in clinical deployment. WHBench provides a public, failure-mode-aware benchmark to track safer and more equitable progress in womens health AI.

At the same time, its expected inference cost per successful escalation is more than 80x lower than that of Claude Opus 4.7. We present OPAL, a CPU-resident C++17 graph engine that preserves record identities, relationships, and accepted numerical state between reasoning sessions. Applications evolve that state through defined updates, save canonical checkpoints, and recover continuity after restart. Bounded Local Generator Classes (BLGC) provide the mathematical foundation for this bounded local evolution. On Apple Silicon M2 Pro hardware, the current-engine resident-enhancement P50 measured 0.083 microseconds at 100,000, 1,000,000, and 5,000,000 retained Atomic Memory Vertices (AMVs). A same-session 1M-5M-1M sequence reproduced that median using one frozen binary and 1,024 prepared targets, with every process passing its correctness checks. These measurements cover complete resident-update calls, including validation, indexed lookup, and numerical state mutation. Initialization and storage-growth costs are reported separately. Reliability tests verified event replay, conflict rejection, concurrent calls, allocation-failure handling, and fresh-process recovery with continued operation. Engine-version comparisons produced byte-identical checkpoints and continuation files. The installed PYAMV Python package passed 17 SDK contract checks and 20 workload checks. KINDRED's Model Context Protocol interface passed 22 distinct focused checks covering memory operations, authorization, and transport. Together, these results demonstrate persistent continuity with low recurring local-update costs through five million retained AMVs, providing working interfaces for applications and developers. The architecture keeps accepted memory available while reasoning is idle, allowing applications to invoke models only when tasks require interpretation, planning, or generation.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (221 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2512.02368v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trajectory prediction is essential for safe planning and decision-making in autonomous driving. Map-free prediction improves deployment flexibility by removing the dependence on high-definition maps, but it also loses explicit road-topology and lane-connectivity priors. Consequently, the model must recover stable motion cues from short histories while resolving prospective interaction relations without lane-level guidance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a map-free trajectory prediction framework centered on a novel Goal-Conditioned Expert-Routed Transformer (GCERT). A lightweight intra-agent front-end first decomposes projected historical motion features into a smooth trend and a local detail residual through a centered moving average. Component-specific residual projections transform the two signals before a causal temporal Transformer summarizes their recombined evolution. GCERT employs dual-level expert routing: edge-level relation experts generate interaction-specific messages, while node-level state experts adapt the transformation after message aggregation. Predicted motion goals upgrade the node representations and construct prospective relative-geometry and orientation edge features before the final interaction layer, thereby conditioning attention, relation-specific message generation, and state transformation. GCERT therefore determines not only which neighboring agents should be attended to, but also what relation-specific information should be transmitted and how the aggregated node state should be transformed. The resulting representations are decoded into multimodal future trajectories and jointly optimized with trajectory-regression, mode-classification, and goal-prediction objectives.

In a recent development, arXiv:2511.19218v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly power web-facing applications, including conversational assistants and content services, where open user interaction exposes them to diverse safety threats and adaptive attacks. In particular, jailbreak attackers repeatedly reformulate harmful requests to bypass safety alignment. Although existing studies have concentrated on defending dynamic jailbreaks, they often retain discovered attacks as flat samples and discard information about how those attacks were found. In this paper, we introduce MACE, an MCTS-guided adversarial co-evolution framework that turns search into policy-learning signals for both an attacker and a defender. Its search component, GS-MCTS, explores multi-step compositions of rewriting operators and associates discovered attacks with empirical success frequency and path depth. Its optimization component, AC-TGPO, uses these statistics for difficulty-aware group-relative credit assignment and constructs a temporally asymmetric curriculum from current interactions, pairings between the latest attacker and preceding defender, and attacks that survive a defense update. Thus, MACE connects search structure to both within-round policy optimization and cross-round memory, rather than using MCTS only to generate attacks or treating each round as a flat adversarial dataset. Removing difficulty-aware weighting, asymmetric samples, or persistent hard samples increases defense ASR-LR by 3.7 %, 6.0 %, and 5.0 %, respectively. Across evaluated models, the resulting attacker achieves the highest ASR-LR in all six model--dataset settings, while the defender reduces average ASR-LR from 11.9 % for the best baseline to 8.8 %.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2510.26185v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Training-data influence estimates support data selection and cleansing by predicting the effects of removing individual examples. The standard multi-epoch SGD-Influence Estimator (SGD-IE) aggregates contributions from a sample's repeated appearances along the recorded trajectory. When used to approximate finite deletion, it omits an interaction: later removals act on the parameter displacement accumulated from earlier removals. We introduce the Accumulative SGD-Influence Estimator (ACC-SGD-IE) to account for how earlier removals change the effect of removing the same sample again. It uses the sample's Hessian at subsequent appearances to correct the estimated parameter change. Our non-convex analysis shows that this correction removes SGD-IE's additional interaction contribution from the finite-horizon error bound: the omitted interaction produces a local error linear in the accumulated parameter change, while the remaining Taylor remainder is bounded quadratically under Lipschitz-Hessian assumptions. The bounds characterize how training propagates the remaining error. In non-convex experiments across clean and noisy tabular, text, and vision datasets, ACC-SGD-IE reduces validation-loss-change RMSE by 10.8% and improves Jaccard@10% by 15.2% on average relative to SGD-IE. These gains also translate into lower test misclassification rates after data cleansing on MNIST and CIFAR10 at the evaluated removal budgets. On noisy industrial datasets, it reduces aggregate parameter RMS error with a mean relative reduction of 53.4%. We further discuss computational tradeoffs, provide complementary theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation for strongly convex objectives, and explore potential extensions of the accumulative correction mechanism to other influence estimators.

The Economics of AI Foundation Models: Openness, Competition, and Governance

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (295 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2510.15200v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation model developers choose how open to make their models. Greater openness lowers downstream adaptation costs but can also make competing models easier to use. In a two-period model, an incumbent chooses its license fee and openness, a deployer adapts the model for users, and an entrant offers a competing model. Usage builds model-specific experience that lowers the deployer's future adaptation cost, creating a data flywheel that favors continued use of the incumbent. We identify conditions under which optimal openness falls and then rises as learning strengthens. The incumbent moves from full openness and a high fee to restricting openness for retention, then to a low fee that builds enough usage and experience to retain the deployer despite greater openness. A full-openness mandate can induce the incumbent to abandon this low-fee strategy. The higher fee can reduce first-period adaptation despite greater openness. An openness trap arises when this welfare loss exceeds the second-period gain from easier adaptation of the entrant's model. The trap can disappear when experience transfers across models. Full integration eliminates the fee between the incumbent and deployer but commits deployment to the incumbent, potentially forgoing a rival that is cheaper to adapt. Integration raises their joint profit, consumer surplus, and welfare when learning is sufficiently strong, but can lower them when learning is weak. A small usage subsidy can benefit both developers, the deployer, and consumers. It can instead induce a fee increase larger than the subsidy and reduced openness, raising the deployer's net payment per use and adaptation costs. The resulting reduction in adaptation lowers welfare even before subsidy expenditure is deducted. These findings connect AI policy to developers' pricing and openness responses and the portability of deployment experience.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (193 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: TAR: Temporal Anchor-Constrained Reasoning for Video Temporal Grounding

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (193 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2508.07683v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) aims to localize specific video segments corresponding to natural language queries. While recent Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) employ Reinforcement Learning to generate Chains-of-Thought (CoT), they typically rely solely on outcome-based supervision. Consequently, this often leads to hallucinations, where the reasoning process becomes disconnected from the visual content and the final prediction. Existing attempts to mitigate this by relying on external supervision from larger models or separate reward models are computationally expensive and prone to rigid patterns. To address these challenges, we propose TAR (Temporal Anchor-Constrained Reasoning), a framework that introduces the temporal anchor (T-anchor) as a transparent and auditable checkpoint mechanism. T-anchor enforces progressive refinement within the CoT, compelling the model to continuously ground its intermediate thoughts in visual evidence and iteratively calibrate temporal predictions, thereby significantly enhancing the faithfulness and autonomy of the reasoning process and final accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a bootstrapping paradigm that automatically harvests high-quality CoT data using only a standard 7B model, eliminating the dependency on ultra-large models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAR achieves state-of-the-art performance and generates faithful, autonomous, and progressively refined reasoning traces.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has been recognized as a Leader and positioned furthest in vision in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems (Cloud ODBMS).
  • Industry observers note that this recognition comes as we cross into the era of agentic AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Google has been recognized as a Leader and positioned furthest in vision in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems (Cloud ODBMS).

Industry observers note that this recognition comes as we cross into the era of agentic AI. Leading enterprises are in their journey of deploying autonomous agents to transform core business functions. At the center is data, the fuel for AI. In our view, this recognition from Gartner — particularly our placement furthest for Completeness of Vision — builds on the August 2026 Gartner® report, AI Vendor Race: Google Is the Company to Beat in Data Platforms for AI. Together, we believe this validates our long-standing belief that the future of operational data is unified, open, and inseparable from the AI layer. In our opinion, this is the blueprint for what we call the Agentic Data Cloud.

Powering a true System of Action through the Agentic Data Cloud requires operational data to be unified, open, and inseparable from the AI tier. We deliver on this across our operational databases by converging transaction processing and analytics in a single engine, while leveraging Google's full-stack AI advantage to integrate Google DeepMind models and vector indexing directly into the core engine over our AI Hypercomputer. Furthermore, we define openness not just through 100% PostgreSQL compatibility and open Apache Iceberg formats, but by providing borderless access to data across other clouds and environments without requiring complete data replication. This eliminates operational friction and costly data movement, providing the low-latency, planet-scale foundation needed to power trusted autonomous agents with confidence.

The Agentic Data Cloud is engineered from the ground up to minimize the complexity and hidden costs of the agentic era. Let's review the core benefits enterprises realize when operating on Google Cloud operational databases, along with our latest innovations to help you thrive in the agentic era.

Industry observers note that our operational database portfolio, anchored by Spanner and AlloyDB, integrates AI natively within the database engine. In AlloyDB, auto vector embeddings and auto vector indexing automatically generate, maintain, and self-tune vector data using simple SQL commands, eliminating complex ETL pipelines. Furthermore, built-in support for Google DeepMind models such as TimesFM enables zero-shot time-series forecasting directly in SQL. With Spanner, organizations can combine full-text, vector, and graph capabilities in a single database to power complex multi-model agentic workflows and context-aware applications with enterprise-grade availability.

In the companion 2026 Gartner® Critical Capabilities for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems report, Google’s operational database portfolio was evaluated as Google (Spanner) and Google (AlloyDB) for the following use cases.

Industry observers note that agentic AI Operations use case: Google was ranked first among all evaluated vendors, with Google (Spanner) ranking #1 and Google (AlloyDB) ranking #2. Capabilities such as natively built AI functions provide developers the ability to bring the power of foundational models within operational databases.

In a recent development, OLTP Transactions use case: Google (Spanner) placed #2 among all evaluated vendors. Spanner's horizontal scalability with full interoperability between various modalities and no-compromise strong consistency enables differentiated experiences.

In addition, Google (Spanner) placed among the 3 highest-scoring vendors across all 4 evaluated use cases in the report, which we believe demonstrates the breadth of workloads it supports across transactional, analytical, NoSQL, and agentic AI scenarios.

According to recent reports, your organization's ability to take advantage of AI depends directly on your enterprise data strategy. Autonomous agents require a modern data foundation that pairs high-performance transactional processing with in-database intelligence and vector capabilities. Google Cloud continues to set the benchmark for enterprise PostgreSQL, delivering high performance and seamless scalability, 100% PostgreSQL compatibility, and enterprise-grade reliability and security, built for agents with AlloyDB for PostgreSQL.

In a recent development, A recent component of this data and AI foundation is PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB. Autonomous agents require real-time data to reason effectively, but their unpredictable and bursty query patterns can degrade performance if not isolated from operational systems. Purpose-built for this challenge, AlloyDB enables real-time data access with complete compute and I/O isolation. Powered by Google’s Colossus distributed storage, it dynamically provisions sandboxed reader instances in seconds—scaling to thousands of nodes, up to 3 million queries per second, and over 8 million IOPS—and scales back to zero when tasks finish. Paired with direct Iceberg access, agents can seamlessly operate across both live transactional data and analytical lakehouse tables in place with zero ETL.

Sources indicate that traditional databases have struggled to keep up with the velocity of AI development, burdened by slow provisioning, CI/CD bottlenecks, and high idle infrastructure costs. AlloyDB Express solves this with an ultra-fast, cost-effective PostgreSQL configuration purpose-built for AI coding agents, rapid prototyping, and ephemeral developer environments. Instances spin up in under two seconds and automatically scale to zero when idle, letting developers and agents iterate rapidly without paying for unused compute. When an application is ready for production, AlloyDB Express provides a seamless, one-click in-place upgrade to AlloyDB—unlocking enterprise-grade scale, high availability, and security while preserving all schemas, data, and connection endpoints.

It has been revealed that spanner's unified multi-model architecture converges relational, graph, vector, and key-value capabilities within a single, planet-scale operational foundation. Graph database structures have swiftly become essential for agentic workloads due to their ability to model complex, interconnected enterprise knowledge and relationships in real time. Spanner Graph enables consumers to execute 14 popular graph algorithms — spanning centrality, community detection, similarity, and path finding — directly through the ISO Graph Query Language (GQL). To prevent performance degradation on production workloads, these algorithms run on a fully managed, isolated compute environment while Data Boost serverlessly transfers graph data. This zero-ETL architecture delivers deep structural analytics and high-performance graph processing without impacting live transactional performance.

Spanner’s columnar engine enables lightweight analytics on the most recent updated data in Spanner. Large analytical queries that require joining analytical data in BigQuery with the latest operational data from Spanner are done leveraging Data Boost, which ensures no impact to  Spanner’s transactional workloads. Complementing these capabilities, the recent launch of Spanner queues brings native transactional messaging directly into Spanner, enabling teams to manage asynchronous background work and orchestrate complex, multi-agent workflows without dual-write complexity.

This unified data ecosystem bridges the gap between intelligence and execution, allowing automated insights to immediately trigger real-time actions back into your critical business applications and operational workflows.

To prevent vendor lock-in and help ensure their long-term viability, enterprise AI deployments require a foundation of open standards and hybrid deployment flexibility. Google Cloud operational databases empower teams to run critical workloads across any environment.

In a recent development, at the foundation of this borderless architecture, Google Cloud databases integrate into the lakehouse ecosystem by delivering unified, zero-ETL access to operational and analytical data. Through native support for open table formats like Apache Iceberg, operational databases such as AlloyDB and Spanner bridge real-time transaction processing with lakehouse analytics. This enables autonomous agents to query, reason over, and act upon live enterprise data instantly across hybrid and multi-cloud environments, minimizing data silos while maintaining strict governance, transactional consistency, and planet-scale performance.

Recent findings suggest that with AlloyDB Omni and Spanner Omni, enterprises can extend Google's advanced operational database capabilities to on-premises environments, multi-cloud deployments, and air-gapped sovereign setups via Google Distributed Cloud (GDC). This helps ensure full operational consistency, compliance, and sovereignty without sacrificing performance or developer velocity.

In a recent development, our database portfolio has also received broader industry recognition. Recently, Google was also named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Operational Databases 2026 Vendor Assessment.

“Consider Google AlloyDB when standardizing on PostgreSQL with deeply integrated AI is a priority, particularly for organizations building AI-driven search, retrieval, and agentic applications on live operational data. The platform suits enterprises that want converged transactional and analytical processing in a single engine, enterprise-grade security, and the flexibility to run the same engine across managed cloud, self-managed, and multicloud environments through AlloyDB Omni. Organizations seeking an AI-native operational database backed by Google's ecosystem will find AlloyDB a practical option for balancing modernization, AI readiness, and operational simplicity.”.

Across Spanner and AlloyDB, we believe this recognition reinforces our mission to deliver a true System of Action built to power autonomous enterprise agents at scale.

To learn more about our placement and how we believe we innovate on behalf of our customers, download the complimentary 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Database Management Systems report.

#8579. Tech Report: QUTCC: Quantile Uncertainty Training and Conformal Calibration for Imaging Inverse Problems

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (223 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: QUTCC: Quantile Uncertainty Training and Conformal Calibration for Imaging Inverse Problems

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (223 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2507.14760v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While deep learning offers tremendous promise for scientific and medical imaging, any failures and hallucinations (predictions that do not coincide with reality) are hard to pinpoint and can have serious downstream consequences. Uncertainty estimation techniques, such as conformal prediction, can help by predicting statistically valid error bars for a model's prediction. However, popular conformal prediction methods were not designed for high-dimensional image-valued problems and do not take into account spatial correlations within an image during conformal calibration, resulting in larger-than-necessary uncertainty intervals. We propose a practical simultaneous quantile regression method that enables non-linear, spatially-adaptive scaling during conformal calibration. Our method, QUTCC uses a U-Net architecture with a quantile embedding to learn a full conditional quantile distribution during training, and then leverages this non-linear, learned function for spatially-adaptive conformal calibration. At test time, our method can efficiently estimate uncertainty intervals with pixel-marginal coverage guarantees. In addition, QUTCC can also predict pixel-wise conditional probability density estimates without any built-in distributional assumptions. We evaluate our method on several denoising problems, accelerated magnetic resonance imaging, and quantitative phase microscopy. Our method consistently produces tighter uncertainty intervals than prior conformal methods at the same coverage level, can predict plausible conditional distributions for different tasks, and in some cases, high-uncertainty regions can help us locate hallucinations in a model's prediction.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (206 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Recursive Learning-Based Virtual Buffering for Analytical Global Placement

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (206 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2506.17247v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Due to the skewed scaling of interconnect versus cell delay in modern technology nodes, placement with buffer porosity (i.e., cell density) awareness is essential for timing closure in physical synthesis flows. However, existing approaches face two key challenges: (i) traditional van Ginneken-Lillis-style buffering approaches are computationally expensive during global placement; and (ii) machine learning-based approaches, such as BufFormer, lack a thorough consideration of Electrical Rule Check (ERC) violations and fail to "close the loop" back into the physical design flow. In this work, we propose MLBuf-RePlAce, the first open-source learning-driven virtual buffering-aware analytical global placement framework, built on top of the OpenROAD infrastructure. MLBuf-RePlAce adopts an efficient recursive learning-based generative buffering approach to predict buffer types and locations, addressing ERC violations during global placement. We compare MLBuf-RePlAce against the default virtual buffering-based timing-driven global placer in OpenROAD, using open-source testcases from the TILOS MacroPlacement and OpenROAD-flow-scripts repositories. Without degradation of post-route power, MLBuf-RePlAce achieves (maximum, average) improvements of (56%, 31%) in total negative slack (TNS) within the open-source OpenROAD flow. When evaluated by completion in a commercial flow, MLBuf-RePlAce achieves (maximum, average) improvements of (53%, 28%) in TNS with an average of 0.2% improvement in post-route power.
